title: A blessing at every meal
hookLine: one blessing before, one thanks after
tomorrow: a little box with a slot sits in the kitchen. what goes in it?

cards: Lunch eaten standing at the counter, one hand on the sandwich, the other scrolling. Done in minutes, forgotten by dinner.

Nobody at that counter is doing anything wrong; the food just came and went without anyone noticing it arrive. Jewish tradition puts a small frame around every meal: one blessing before, and a thank-you after.
The one before is easy to remember; you're hungry. So why does the Torah ask for one after?

teach.b: Because full is when you forget.
Deuteronomy puts it plainly: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat, be satisfied, then bless.
The very next verses warn against forgetting once you've eaten your fill. That's the root of the grace after meals, the thank-you said when the plate is empty.
Look at what it thanks God for: the good land, not just lunch. When the plate is empty, the thank-you reaches past the plate. The blessing before is the rabbis' addition.
The Talmud teaches that enjoying anything of this world without a blessing is like taking without asking.
So before bread, Jews say hamotzi: blessed are You, who brings forth bread from the earth.
Notice the picture: not bread from a bakery, but from the earth, as if the whole chain, soil, rain, farmer, baker, is being thanked at once.
Other foods have their own short blessings too, for fruit, for wine, for everything else, so no snack falls outside the frame. One frame, two edges. Hungry, you remember; full, you remember again.
And every meal in between is blessed.

how: Before eating bread, Jews say hamotzi, and after a meal with bread, Birkat Hamazon, the grace after meals, sometimes sung together at the table; other foods have their own short blessings before and after.

games.q: what does “a blessing at every meal” mean?
o: a blessing before eating and a thank-you after
a toast raised at the start of a holiday dinner
a rule to eat only foods blessed by a rabbi

games.q: two weeks of lines — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah's food blessing comes before the meal
Deuteronomy says eat, be satisfied, and bless: the Torah's blessing comes after. the one before is the rabbis'.
hamotzi thanks God for bringing bread from the earth
not from a bakery: the whole chain, soil to baker, in one line.
Rabbi Shimon says a fixed prayer is fine even when it goes rote
he warns against prayer gone rote; Shammai says fix a time. a rule of three lines keeps both.

games.q: the holiday meal is over, everyone's stuffed, and the kids are already heading for the couch. by Deuteronomy, which moment needs the blessing most?
o: now, while everyone's full, because full is when you forget.
the start only, since thanks counts most when you're hungry.
neither; a big family meal is a blessing on its own.
games.why: eat, be satisfied, and bless: the Torah's blessing comes when you're full, and the next verses warn against forgetting.

practice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one small bite or sip, slowly, and taste it all the way through, the way you would taste something for the first time.
If you say blessings, say the one before; if not, name one person in the chain that brought it to you. When it's gone, say a short thank-you, out loud, for being satisfied, and notice that you are.

wordCard.voice: A blessing at every meal: hamotzi before bread, and grace after, from Deuteronomy's eat, be satisfied, and bless. A frame around every meal, so that none of them simply disappears.

orig.note: Hebrew: who brings forth, from the blessing over bread: who brings forth bread from the earth.

carryVoice: Keep it close: every meal blessed, hungry and full. Two weeks, done; the game round's next.
